usage: I feel sick (lit. my body hurts)
the default way to say you're unwell; note the particle 이, not 을
softer/vaguer than 아파요; good for general malaise or even feeling low
set farewell when it's cold or someone's sick; 몸 + 조심하다 fused
I feel sluggish (lit. my body is heavy)
tiredness/heaviness, not literal weight; contrast 살이 쪘어요 for weight
examples: 오늘은 몸이 좀 피곤해요.
I'm a bit tired today.
simple: 몸이 + adjective is the basic frame for how your body feels
몸이 아파서 회사에 못 갔어요.
I was sick, so I couldn't go to work.
everyday: 아파서 (A-아서) gives the reason; pair with 못 가다
요즘 무리해서 그런지 몸이 자꾸 안 좋아요.
Maybe because I've been overdoing it, I keep feeling under the weather lately.
real-life: 안 좋다 for ongoing vague unwellness, 자꾸 = keeps happening
nuance: 몸 is the physical body taken as a whole, and crucially it's also the word Koreans reach for to describe how they FEEL: 몸이 아파요 (sick) and 몸이 안 좋아요 (off/unwell) are the everyday health phrases. The near-synonym is the Sino-Korean 신체(身體, 'body-substance'), but 신체 is clinical/official — 신체검사 (physical exam), 신체 활동 (physical activity) — and sounds stiff if you use it about yourself, so say 몸. Habitual collocations: 몸이 아프다, 몸이 안 좋다, 몸이 피곤하다, 몸이 무겁다, 몸조심하다, 몸이 약하다 (to have a weak constitution). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the verb: you say 몸이 아프다 ('the body is sick'), so the body is the SUBJECT (이/가) — never 몸을 아파요. Also don't directly translate 'my body is heavy' as a weight statement; 몸이 무겁다 means you feel sluggish/lethargic, not that you weigh a lot.

Using 신체 in casual speech, e.g. 신체가 아파요. That sounds like a medical chart; everyday Korean is 몸이 아파요.
Reading 몸이 무거워요 as 'I'm overweight.' It means you feel heavy/sluggish; weight gain is 살이 쪘어요.

usage: the standard line; 살이 찌다, subject particle 이, never 살을 쪘어요
intransitive 빠지다 = it fell off on its own
transitive 빼다 = you actively remove it; takes 을
compound 배(belly) + 살; also 옆구리살 love handles, 허벅지살 thigh fat
examples: 요즘 살이 좀 쪘어요.
I've gained a little weight lately.
simple: 살이 찌다 is the core intransitive frame
여름 전에 살을 빼고 싶어요.
I want to lose weight before summer.
everyday: 살을 빼다 (transitive, deliberate) + -고 싶다
다이어트를 해도 살이 잘 안 빠져서 스트레스예요.
Even though I diet, the weight just won't come off, so it's stressful.
real-life: 살이 빠지다 (it comes off by itself) vs 살을 빼다 (you remove it)
nuance: 살 is the soft flesh of the body, and in daily life it's the word for body fat / weight: 살이 찌다 (put on weight) and its pair 살이 빠지다 / 살을 빼다 (lose weight). The synonym contrast that trips learners is 살 vs the Sino-Korean 체중(體重, 'body-weight'): 체중 is the number on the scale (체중을 재다 = to measure one's weight, 체중 50kg), while 살 is the fat itself that you gain, lose, or pinch — in conversation Koreans overwhelmingly say 살, not 체중. Note also 살 ≠ 피부: 살 is the fleshy substance, 피부 is the skin's surface. Watch the transitivity pair: 빠지다 is intransitive ('fat falls off' — 살이 빠지다, subject 이) but 빼다 is transitive ('you take the fat off' — 살을 빼다, object 을); mixing the particles is the classic mistake. Common collocations: 살이 찌다/빠지다, 살을 빼다, 살이 많다, 뱃살, 살이 쪄서. (Same syllable 살 also means 'years of age' as a counter, and homophone-adjacent 쌀 is uncooked rice — different tense ㅆ.)

Using 체중 in casual chat: 체중이 쪘어요. Say 살이 쪘어요; 체중 is the formal scale-number word.

usage: I'm bleeding (lit. blood is coming out)
the must-know phrase; verb is 나다, particle 이/가
멈추다 = to stop; the natural pair to 피가 나다
코(nose) + 피; 코피가 나다 = to get a nosebleed
흘리다 = to spill; more dramatic/literary than 피가 나다
examples: 손에서 피가 나요.
My hand is bleeding.
simple: location + 에서 (out of) + 피가 나다
넘어져서 무릎에서 피가 났어요.
I fell and my knee bled.
everyday: past 났어요; 에서 marks where blood emerges
피만 봐도 어지러워서 주사를 잘 못 맞아요.
Just the sight of blood makes me dizzy, so I'm bad with shots.
real-life: 피만 봐도 (even just seeing blood) + 어지럽다
nuance: 피 is the plain, native everyday word for blood — what you say the instant you cut yourself: 피가 나요 (I'm bleeding) is the single most useful phrase here. The synonym contrast is with the Sino-Korean 혈액(血液, 'blood-fluid'): 혈액 is the technical/medical register you see on forms and signs — 혈액형 (blood type), 헌혈 (blood donation, 獻血), 혈액 검사 (blood test) — whereas in speech about a scrape you always use 피. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb: 'blood comes out' uses 나다 (to come out/occur), so 피가 나다 — not 피가 오다 (오다 is 'come [toward me]' and is wrong here). Mark where the blood emerges with 에서 (from a place): 코에서 피가 나요. Also note 피 is normally uncountable — don't pluralize it. Handy collocations: 피가 나다, 피가 멈추다, 피를 흘리다, 코피가 나다, 피를 뽑다 (to draw blood, at a clinic).

usage: 트다 → 텄어요; the seasonal winter complaint
the dictionary form; same 트다 used for chapped hands
깨물다 = to bite down; gesture of enduring or nervousness
바르다 = to spread on; 립밤을 바르다
examples: 겨울에는 입술이 잘 말라요.
My lips get dry easily in winter.
simple: 입술이 마르다 (to go dry); 잘 = easily/often
입술이 터서 립밤을 발랐어요.
My lips were chapped, so I put on lip balm.
everyday: 터서 (트다 + 아서, reason) + 바르다
긴장하면 저도 모르게 입술을 깨물어요.
When I'm nervous I bite my lip without realizing it.
real-life: habit + 저도 모르게 (without even knowing it)
nuance: 입술 means the lips, and it's transparently built from 입 (mouth/opening) + 술 — but the contrast to nail down is 입 vs 입술: 입 is the whole mouth (you eat, speak, and open your 입), while 입술 is specifically the two lip rims (you apply balm to, bite, or chap your 입술). It surfaces constantly in two contexts: winter skin (입술이 마르다 / 입술이 트다, chapped lips) and cosmetics (입술에 립스틱/립밤을 바르다). A frequent learner error is reaching for 입 when you mean the lips — 입이 텄어요 sounds odd; chapping happens to the 입술. Lips are inherently a pair, so Korean leaves them singular: say 입술, not 입술들. Useful collocations: 입술이 마르다, 입술이 트다, 입술을 깨물다, 입술을 바르다, 입술이 부르트다 (to blister, e.g. a cold sore).

Pluralizing as 입술들. Lips are treated as a single paired item; just say 입술.
Saying 입술을 깨물었다 vs 깨물다 confusion aside, learners often pick 물다 alone (to bite/hold in mouth). For the lip-biting gesture it's 깨물다 (bite down).

usage: 데다 = to get burned/scalded; 뜨거운 거에 혀를 데다
깨물다 = to bite down; accidental while eating or talking
꼬이다 = to twist; when drunk or nervous, 발음이 새다 nearby
차다 here = to click; gesture of disapproval/pity
examples: 혀로 맛을 느껴요.
We taste with our tongue.
simple: 혀로 (with the tongue, instrument 로) + 맛 (taste)
뜨거운 국을 먹다가 혀를 데었어요.
I burned my tongue eating hot soup.
everyday: V-다가 (mid-action) + 혀를 데다
발음이 어려워서 혀가 자꾸 꼬여요.
The pronunciation is hard, so my tongue keeps getting twisted.
real-life: idiomatic 혀가 꼬이다 for fumbling speech
nuance: 혀 is the tongue — the organ you taste, swallow, and articulate sounds with. The key contrast for learners is 혀 (the physical organ) vs 맛 (taste, the sensation): you taste WITH your 혀, but the act 'to taste/sample food' is 맛을 보다, never 혀를 보다. Most common beginner sentences: 혀를 데었어요 (I burned my tongue) and 혀를 깨물었어요 (I bit my tongue), both very real mishaps. It also lives in vivid idioms — 혀가 꼬이다 (slur your words, e.g. when drunk) and 혀를 차다 (click your tongue in disapproval, 'tsk'). Pronunciation pitfall for English speakers: 혀 is one syllable with the vowel 여 (roughly 'hyŏ'/'hyuh'), a y-glide + ŏ — don't flatten it to 'ha' or stretch it into two beats; and keep it distinct from 햐/혜. Mark the instrument with 로/으로: 혀로 핥다 (to lick with the tongue). Collocations: 혀를 데다, 혀를 깨물다, 혀로 핥다, 혀가 꼬이다, 혀를 차다.

Using 자르다 (to cut) for biting the tongue: 혀를 잘랐어요. Accidentally biting it is 혀를 깨물었어요 (bit down).

usage: 깎다 is the idiomatic verb (also for peeling, haircuts); not 자르다
자라다 = to grow; 손톱이 빨리 자라요
발(foot) + 톱; the sibling word, also clipped with 깎다
물어뜯다 = to gnaw; the nervous-habit verb
examples: 손톱이 길어서 깎았어요.
My nails were long, so I clipped them.
simple: 손톱이 길다 + 깎다 (clip)
손톱에 매니큐어를 발랐어요.
I painted my nails.
everyday: 손톱에 (on the nails, 에) + 바르다
문에 부딪혀서 손톱이 부러졌어요.
I hit it on the door and my nail broke.
real-life: 부러지다 (snap, for rigid things) for a cracked nail
nuance: 손톱 is a fingernail — 손 (hand) + 톱 — and you should bank it together with its mirror word 발톱 (toenail). The verb to memorize is 깎다 (to shave/clip), the very same verb Koreans use for peeling an apple (사과를 깎다) and getting a haircut (머리를 깎다); for trimming nails it's 손톱을 깎다, and learners who reach for 자르다 (to cut [in two]) sound off — 자르다 suggests cutting something through, while 깎다 means shaving a thin layer. To paint nails you 'spread' polish on them: 손톱에 매니큐어를 바르다 (note 에 for the surface). A broken nail uses 부러지다 (to snap), the verb for rigid things. Don't confuse 손톱 (fingernail) with 발톱 (toenail) — only the 손/발 (hand/foot) differs — and keep it one word with no space (손톱, not 손 톱). The 톱 here is unrelated in meaning to 톱 'a saw'; just treat 손톱/발톱 as fixed words. Collocations: 손톱을 깎다, 손톱이 자라다, 손톱이 부러지다, 손톱을 물어뜯다.

usage: 진하다 = dense/dark (also of coffee, makeup); opposite 연하다 light
그리다 = to draw; the standard makeup verb
속(inner) + 눈썹; 속눈썹이 길다 = long lashes
examples: 눈썹이 진하고 예뻐요.
Your eyebrows are dark and pretty.
simple: 눈썹이 + 진하다 (dark/thick)
거울을 보면서 눈썹을 그렸어요.
I filled in my eyebrows looking in the mirror.
everyday: -면서 (while) + 눈썹을 그리다
눈썹 위에 작은 점이 하나 있어요.
I have a little mole above my eyebrow.
real-life: 눈썹 위에 (above, position 위 + 에) + 점이 있다
nuance: 눈썹 is the eyebrow — 눈 (eye) + 썹 — and the must-pair word is 속눈썹 (eyelashes), where 속 means 'inner/inside,' so the lashes are framed as the 'inner brow.' Keep three things separate: 눈 (the eye itself), 눈썹 (the brow ridge of hair above), and 속눈썹 (the lashes on the lid) — calling lashes 눈썹 is the usual slip. The describing adjective is 진하다 (dark/dense, opposite 연하다 'light'), the same word for strong coffee or heavy makeup, so 눈썹이 진하다 = thick, dark brows. In makeup talk the verb is 그리다 (to draw) — 눈썹을 그리다 means to pencil/fill them in, and 눈썹을 다듬다 means to trim/shape them. To place a feature relative to the brow, use a position noun + 에: 눈썹 위에 (above the brow). Eyebrows aren't pluralized with 들. Collocations: 눈썹이 진하다, 눈썹을 그리다, 눈썹을 다듬다, 속눈썹이 길다.

usage: to be tall (lit. height is big)
uses 크다 not 길다; 키가 커요
작다 (small), the opposite; never 짧다 for a person's height
casual; more formal 키가 어떻게 되세요?
past 컸다 = grew; 키가 많이 컸어요 = grew a lot
examples: 제 친구는 키가 커요.
My friend is tall.
simple: 키가 크다, the core 'tall' frame
저는 키가 작은 편이에요.
I'm on the shorter side.
everyday: -은 편이다 (tend toward) softens the statement
1년 사이에 동생 키가 많이 컸어요.
My younger sibling grew a lot taller in a year.
real-life: 키가 크다 in past = grew; 사이에 = in the span of
nuance: 키 is a person's height/stature, and the make-or-break point is which adjective it takes: Korean treats height as BIG vs SMALL, so it's 키가 크다 (tall) and 키가 작다 (short) — never 키가 길다 ('long') or 키가 짧다 ('short [in length]'), which are the natural-but-wrong direct translations from English. The same 크다 in the past tense doubles as 'grew': 키가 컸어요 means 'grew taller,' so context decides between 'is tall' and 'grew.' To ask height, casual speech is 키가 몇이에요? and polite is 키가 어떻게 되세요?. This 키 (height) is a separate word from the loanword 키 ('key') and from 키 'rudder/oar' — same spelling, told apart by context. Note height is the subject (키가...), with the person marked by 은/는 (저는 키가 커요 = 'as for me, height is big'). Collocations: 키가 크다, 키가 작다, 키가 크다=grow, 키를 재다 (to measure height), 키 순서 (height order).

usage: lit. 'voice doesn't come out'; from a cold or shouting
낮추다 = to lower (volume or pitch); 목소리를 높이다 = raise it
examples: 그 가수는 목소리가 정말 좋아요.
That singer has a really nice voice.
simple: 목소리가 좋다, the basic compliment frame
감기에 걸려서 목소리가 안 나와요.
I have a cold, so I've lost my voice.
everyday: 감기에 걸리다 (catch a cold) + 목소리가 안 나오다
여기 도서관이니까 목소리 좀 낮춰 주세요.
This is a library, so please lower your voice.
real-life: -니까 (reason) + 목소리를 낮추다 as a polite request
nuance: 목소리 is the (human) voice, transparently 목 (throat/neck) + 소리 (sound) — literally 'throat-sound.' The synonym contrast is 목소리 vs plain 소리: 소리 is ANY sound (a noise, a bang, music), whereas 목소리 is specifically a person's vocal sound, so 'I like her voice' must be 목소리가 좋다, not 소리가 좋다. It serves both compliments (목소리가 좋다) and health (감기 때문에 목소리가 안 나와요 = losing your voice). The sharp learner pitfall is loud vs high: volume is 크다/작다 (목소리가 크다 = loud), but PITCH is 높다/낮다 (목소리가 높다 = high-pitched). English 'a loud voice' tempts people into 목소리가 높아요, which actually says 'high-pitched' — use 목소리가 커요 for loud. To adjust volume, 목소리를 높이다/낮추다 (raise/lower). Collocations: 목소리가 좋다, 목소리가 크다/작다, 목소리가 안 나오다, 목소리를 낮추다, 목소리가 잠기다 (to go hoarse).

usage: 보이다 = to be visible; 옷이 짧아서 배꼽이 보여요
idiom: 'laugh till your navel falls out'; 빠지게 = to the point of falling out
examples: 아기 배꼽이 정말 작고 귀여워요.
The baby's belly button is really small and cute.
simple: 배꼽이 + adjective, plain description
옷이 짧아서 배꼽이 살짝 보여요.
The top is short, so my belly button shows a little.
everyday: 짧아서 (reason) + 배꼽이 보이다, 살짝 = slightly
어제 그 영상 보고 배꼽 빠지게 웃었어요.
I laughed so hard at that video yesterday.
real-life: the 배꼽 빠지게 웃다 idiom in casual past speech
nuance: 배꼽 is the belly button/navel, the small point sitting on the 배 (belly/stomach) — so don't blur 배꼽 (just the navel) with 배 (the whole abdomen): 배가 아파요 is a stomachache, but 배꼽이 아파요 would specifically be the navel. It's a friendly, concrete word that powers some very common expressions: the idiom 배꼽(이) 빠지게 웃다 (to laugh so hard 'your navel falls out' — i.e. split your sides), the fashion word 배꼽티 (crop top), and the joke 배꼽시계 (your stomach 'clock' announcing it's mealtime). Spelling pitfall for learners: it ends in a tense ㄲ — 배꼽, not 배곱 — and it's one word. Because it's a single point, it isn't pluralized. Useful collocations: 배꼽이 보이다, 배꼽이 나오다 (an 'outie'/protruding navel), 배꼽 빠지게 웃다, 배꼽티를 입다.

usage: 쥐다 = to grip/close the hand; not 잡다 (grab an object)
주먹(fist) + 밥(rice); hand-pressed, a lunchbox staple
날리다 = to send flying; informal/violent register
examples: 사과가 주먹만 해요.
The apple is about the size of a fist.
simple: 주먹만 하다 as a size yardstick
화가 나서 주먹을 꽉 쥐었어요.
I got angry and clenched my fist tight.
everyday: 꽉 (tightly) + 주먹을 쥐다
점심으로 참치 주먹밥을 만들어 먹었어요.
I made tuna rice balls for lunch.
real-life: the compound 주먹밥 in a cooking context
nuance: 주먹 is a clenched fist — the closed hand, as opposed to 손, the hand in general (open or whole). The verb that goes with it is 쥐다 (to grip / close the hand around): 주먹을 쥐다 = to make a fist, often intensified by 꽉 (tightly). Learners often substitute 잡다 (to grab/hold an object), but 잡다 needs a thing to grab — for closing your own hand into a fist it's 쥐다, not 잡다. 주먹 doubles as a vivid size unit (주먹만 하다 = 'as big as a fist'), and it builds the very common food word 주먹밥 (hand-pressed rice ball — 주먹 + 밥). In rougher, informal contexts it heads fight vocabulary: 주먹을 날리다 (throw a punch), 주먹다짐 (a fistfight), and figuratively 주먹구구 (rough/sloppy estimation). Collocations: 주먹을 쥐다, 주먹을 꽉 쥐다, 주먹만 하다, 주먹밥, 주먹을 날리다.

usage: 손(hand) + 바닥(flat bottom surface); the opposite side of 손등
for the back of the hand to be dry
to apply on the back of the hand
바르다 = to spread on; 핸드크림을 바르다
to wipe with the back of the hand
examples: 겨울에 손등이 너무 건조해요.
The backs of my hands are so dry in winter.
simple: 손등이 + 건조하다
손등에 핸드크림을 발랐어요.
I put hand cream on the back of my hand.
everyday: 손등에 (on, surface 에) + 바르다
땀이 나서 손등으로 이마를 쓱 닦았어요.
I was sweating, so I quickly wiped my forehead with the back of my hand.
real-life: 손등으로 (instrument 으로) + 닦다; 쓱 = with a swipe
nuance: 손등 is the back of the hand, a compound of 손 (hand) + 등 (back) — the very same 등 that means the back of the body, so it literally reads 'hand-back.' Its anatomical opposite, which you should learn as a pair, is 손바닥 (palm), from 손 + 바닥 ('flat bottom/floor surface'); the two name the two faces of the hand and learners often mix them up. Notice how Korean builds body parts with 등 and 바닥: 발등 (top of the foot) and 발바닥 (sole) work identically — a neat pattern to lock in together. Grammar-wise, things sit ON the 손등 with 에 (손등에 크림을 바르다), but when the back of the hand is the TOOL you act with, use 으로 (손등으로 닦다, wipe with it). It's a single word — write 손등, not 손 등. Collocations: 손등이 건조하다, 손등에 바르다, 손등으로 닦다, 손등에 핏줄이 보이다 (veins showing on the back of the hand).

usage: the short, far more common everyday version
for the throat to sting/be raw
따갑다 = to sting/prickle; that scratchy cold feeling
to get stuck in the throat
걸리다 = to get caught; 가시가 목구멍에 걸렸어요
examples: 감기에 걸려서 목이 아파요.
I caught a cold and my throat hurts.
simple: the everyday short form 목이 아프다
목구멍이 따가워서 따뜻한 물을 마셨어요.
My throat was raw, so I drank warm water.
everyday: 목구멍이 따갑다 + reason -아서
생선 가시가 목구멍에 걸려서 병원에 갔어요.
A fish bone got stuck in my throat, so I went to the clinic.
real-life: 목구멍에 걸리다; precise inner-passage sense
nuance: 목구멍 is the throat as the inner passage/gullet, literally 목 (neck/throat) + 구멍 (hole) — 'throat-hole.' The crucial register/synonym point is 목 vs 목구멍: 목 covers both the neck (the outside) AND the throat, and in everyday speech a sore throat is almost always the short 목이 아파요 — people rarely say 목구멍이 아파요 in casual talk. You reach for 목구멍 when you need to specify the inside cavity: something lodged in it (가시가 목구멍에 걸리다), or a raw, stinging sensation deep inside (목구멍이 따갑다). At the clinic the formal term is the Sino-Korean 인후(咽喉), as in 인후염 (pharyngitis) or 이비인후과 (ENT clinic, 'ear-nose-throat dept'). Collocations: 목구멍이 따갑다, 목구멍에 걸리다, 목이 아프다, 목이 붓다, 목이 잠기다 (to go hoarse).

usage: to be smart (lit. head is good)
casual mental ability uses 머리, not 뇌
쓰다 = to use; can be literal or jokingly 'think hard'
informal: 머릿속이 하얘지다 nearby; blanking out
뇌(腦) + 세포(細胞); 뇌세포가 죽다 = brain cells dying, joking
examples: 사람의 뇌는 정말 신기해요.
The human brain is really fascinating.
simple: 뇌 as the literal organ + 신기하다
잠을 자는 동안 뇌도 쉬어요.
While you sleep, your brain rests too.
everyday: -는 동안 (during) + 뇌가 쉬다
시험 때 너무 긴장하면 뇌가 멈추는 것 같아요.
When I'm too nervous during an exam, it's like my brain freezes.
real-life: informal 뇌가 멈추다 for going blank
nuance: 뇌 is the brain as the physical organ — Sino-Korean 腦 ('brain') — and it's the right word for anatomy, health, and science: 뇌 수술 (brain surgery), 뇌세포 (brain cells), 뇌가 손상되다 (the brain is damaged). The key contrast for learners is 뇌 vs 머리: for everyday talk about intelligence, thinking, or memory, Koreans say 머리 (head/mind), NOT 뇌 — 'she's smart' is 머리가 좋다, you 'rack your brain' as 머리를 쓰다, and an idea pops into 머릿속 (inside the head). So reserve 뇌 for the literal organ and use 머리 for mental ability; saying 뇌가 좋다 for 'smart' sounds like a textbook mistranslation. Pronunciation pitfall: 뇌 is a single syllable, the diphthong 외 — roughly 'nö'/'nwe' (close to French eu or a quick 'nweh') — so don't split it into two beats ('no-i') or say 'noy.' Collocations (organ sense): 뇌가 쉬다, 뇌를 쓰다, 뇌 수술, 뇌세포, 뇌가 활성화되다.
